title: For such a time (Esther 4:14)
hook: a Jewish queen risks her life for her people; Jews keep Purim remembering it
carry: for such a time as this

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerusalem fell and the people went into exile. Your line was even exile is not the end. Who far from home did you speak kindly to? Day seven hundred forty.

The story is set far from Jerusalem, in the Persian royal city of Shushan, among Jews still scattered across the empire. A young Jewish woman, Esther, raised by her cousin Mordecai, has become queen. She has kept quiet about who her people are. Then a powerful official, Haman, angry that Mordecai won't bow to him, gets the king to sign an order to destroy the Jews of the whole empire on a single day. Haman picks the day by casting lots. Mordecai sends word to the palace: go to the king. Esther sends word back: anyone who walks in to the king without being called is put to death, unless he holds out his golden scepter. Mordecai's reply is today.
screen: `GO IN UNCALLED, AND YOU MAY DIE.`

segments.voice: Mordecai doesn't flatter her. He tells her the palace won't hide her, and then, in the King James Bible: "For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place." Help will come from somewhere, he says. The only question is whether you'll be part of it. And then the question: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" Who knows. He doesn't claim to be sure. He just asks her to consider that her strange place, a Jewish orphan wearing a Persian crown, might not be an accident. Esther's answer is just as strong. She asks the Jews of the city to fast for her three days, and says she and her maids will fast too. Then: "so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish." She goes in. The king holds out the scepter. And in a complete reversal, Haman ends up on the gallows he built for Mordecai, and the Jews are allowed to defend themselves. The book names the festival that remembers it: "they called these days Purim after the name of Pur," and Pur, the text says, means the lot Haman cast. The book itself asks for days of feasting and joy, sending portions to one another and gifts to the poor, and Jewish tradition keeps Purim by reading the scroll of Esther aloud. Some readers point out that in this book, as the King James Bible prints it, God is never named. And yet Jewish and Christian readers have long heard God at work behind it, through a cousin's question and a queen's nerve.

Here's the practice: find your palace door. Settle, and breathe. Where do you have access that other people don't? A boss who listens to you. A family group chat. A classroom, a committee, a friend who trusts you. Somewhere you could say one true thing that would help someone who can't get in the room. Let one come to mind. Then notice what's keeping you quiet: fear, comfort, not wanting to make it awkward. You don't have to decide anything yet. If you pray, you can bring that door to God. If you don't, just stand in front of it for a while. The bell holds the time.
Purim. The festival named for the lot Haman cast, kept by Jews to remember how Esther went in to the king and her people were saved.
Your line: for such a time as this. Today, speak up once, kindly and clearly, in a place where you have access and someone else doesn't. Day seven hundred forty.

howItsDone: Christians read Esther as scripture and sometimes quote Mordecai's for such a time as this when someone takes on a hard calling; Jews keep Purim each year by reading the scroll of Esther aloud, sending food to friends and giving gifts to the poor.

original.note: Hebrew: lots, the plural of pur. Esther 3:7 says pur is the lot Haman cast to choose the day.

notes: Purim customs (reading the Megillah aloud, noise at Haman's name, mishloach manot, gifts to the poor) described briefly as a neighbor's practice; Esther 9:22 names portions and gifts to the poor. A Jewish reviewer may wish to confirm the description.

'In Esther as the King James Bible prints it, God is never named' refers to the Hebrew-based book; the Greek additions (in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, and the KJV Apocrypha) do name God. Confirm wording, and whether to mention the Greek additions for this broad path.
'Readers, Jewish and Christian, have heard God all through it' is interpretive; confirm.

The reversal (Haman hanged on the gallows built for Mordecai, Jews permitted to defend themselves) summarizes 7:10 and 8:11; the violence of chapter 9 is not described. Confirm the summary is acceptable.

Editor pass: 'the line people still quote' cut; Purim customs now tied to Esther 9:22 (feasting, portions, gifts to the poor) with the scroll reading attributed to Jewish tradition; the noise at Haman's name (not in the cited text) removed from the spoken teach.

Audit: 'a reversal so neat it's almost funny' (said of a hanging) cut to 'a complete reversal'; sweeping 'readers... have heard God all through it' softened to 'have long heard God at work behind it'.
